A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

From Augustus to Nero, see how much you know about ancient Rome's famous leaders with our Roman emperor quiz!

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6554. 21 Easy Thanksgiving Appetizers That'll Impress Without The Stress

Thanksgiving asks a lot of us (and our ovens!). From making the turkey to all of the casseroles and sides, don’t even get me started on dessert. You’ve got a lot on your plate, so we’re trying to make the big turkey day a little easier. Appetizers are my favorite part of the meal: little bites that pack so much flavor and fun into the start of the big feast, so you’ve gotta make them count. We’ve got some clever, simple shortcuts to help you whip up appetizers that will impress your guests without adding to your stress.

Whether you’re looking for quick and easy last-minute options or want something more elaborate, we’ve got something on this list for you. Need more Thanksgiving hosting ideas? Check out our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes and Thanksgiving cocktails!

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

There is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. These would be a fun alternative to biscuits or Parker House rolls at Thanksgiving or another big family meal.

Having multiple Thanksgivings this year? Want to transform your leftovers from one into something incredible for the next? Look no further than this stuffed bread ring—it's gorgeous and super easy, thanks to store-bought crescent roll dough.

With all of the elements of stuffing plus the added flaky and butter benefits of biscuits, this pull-apart stuffing bread just might start a tug-of-war situation at your table when you grab for a slice.

It’s a tail as old as time: It’s right before Thanksgiving dinner, and your guests don’t want a full meal but are feeling a little peckish. Try a bird of a different feather this year, and serve this festive and impressive fruit and cheese display as the centerpiece of your holiday app table.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. Preparing these potato skins is simple; all you need for this recipe are Thanksgiving leftovers and a few additional pantry staples: potatoes and cheddar cheese.

It’s hard to find a party appetizer that’s more beloved than a cheese log—or its alternate form, the cheese ball. Here, dried sweetened cranberries, walnuts, and fresh thyme conjure a holiday feeling, while a little honey complements the sweet-tart fruit.

These are a fan favorite every fall. They always disappear within minutes, probably because the combo of salty, creamy brie, sweet-tart cranberry sauce, and crunchy pecans is PERFECT.

Fall desserts may get all the attention once autumn comes around, but I'm here to say that seasonal appetizers deserve their share of the spotlight—especially these adorable pizza-stuffed pumpkins. Stuffed with creamy ricotta, these biscuit-based bites are baked to golden perfection before being brushed with a flavor-packed garlic butter.

Just like our famous cranberry brie bites, these little guys are hard to put down! They're the perfect amount of sweet and savory, so you can serve them before or after the big meal.

Sausage Stuffing Bites With Cranberry Sauce

Stuffing, inside the turkey or out, is a Thanksgiving staple. The only thing better? MORE. STUFFING. Enter this bite-sized, stuffing-centered appetizer with a tangy, three-ingredient dipping sauce (just cranberry sauce, honey, and Dijon).

Even if you're not serving turkey this Thanksgiving doesn't mean you can't get in on the theme. Enter: this adorable cheeseball. We used carrots, pecans, pretzels, and bell peppers to create the iconic look, but feel free to substitute them with different ingredients for what you have on hand. Serve it with crackers and use the decorations as dippers too!

These sweet potato bites have a crunchy, herbaceous crust, with a sweet, silky inside that, when topped with a light drizzle of honey, will have you craving them again and again. Once you bite through the crust, the sweet potato mixes with that melted, nutty Gruyère for a dream flavor combination that works SO well.

Cranberry brie bites are by far one of our favorite appetizers for the holidays, but jalapeño poppers also have place in our hearts too... So why not combine them? The spice of the jalapeño goes so well with the tart cranberries.

To make these, we stuff baby bella mushrooms with garlicky, herby breadcrumbs and plenty of cheese. Stuff them ahead of time and bake them off when you're ready for the most Thanksgiving-friendly appetizer ever.

Pull-apart bread reaches a whole new level, thanks to brie and cranberry sauce. Use your favorite homemade sauce recipes, but store-bought works too if you're short for time.

Little puff pastry squares get topped with caramelized onions and a little crumbled goat cheese for an easy appetizer that always wows. The final step is a light drizzle of honey for that salty sweet combination everyone will love.

If you’re a fan of our cranberry brie bites, we’ve got news for you: There’s a new app in town, and it’s inspired by another fan fave, baked feta pasta. These features the flavors you know and love, all nestled into bite-sized cups of golden crescent roll dough.

There's something very classic about the crescent roll dough flavor, so we tend to gravitate toward it, but puff pastry or even biscuit dough should both work here, too.

Think this sounds like a strange combo? You've gotta trust us on this one. If the aroma of toasted puff pastry, roasted apples, and nutty cheddar cheese doesn’t wake up your spirit… we're not sure what will.

#6553. Maitake “Bacon”

“Maitake is one of the tastiest and most versatile things you’ll find growing at the base of a rotting tree,” writes Alexis Nikole Nelson, better known as the Black Forager, in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! Here, Nelson harnesses the savory, meaty qualities of the mushroom (which also goes by the name hen of the woods) to turn it into little hunks of bacon-y goodness that are salty, smoky, and the tiniest bit sweet.

#6552. Sheet-Pan Cider Vinegar Chicken

Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside.

Arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour.

Meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet.

Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes.

Scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.

#6550. Shake Shack Just Recruited A Very Famous Chocolate Brand For Its Holiday Shakes

There's a whole lot happening under that whipped cream.

The most elaborate of the bunch is the Hazelnut Chocolate Shake, which starts with vanilla frozen custard blended with chocolate-hazelnut spread. That’s poured into a crackable dark chocolate shell before being topped with whipped cream, chopped hazelnuts, crunchy wafer flakes, and a Ferrero Rocher chocolate square.

There’s also the new Butterscotch Crème Brûlée Shake, made with butterscotch crème brûlée frozen custard and finished with whipped cream and honeycomb pieces in the drink, giving a little crunch to go along with all that creaminess.

Even the bags and cups are getting dressed up for the holidays. Shake Shack's packaging this year turns its original Madison Square Park location into a gingerbread house, complete with wreaths and string lights as a cute little nod to where the chain got its start.

The shakes are available for a limited time, although Shake Shack hasn't announced an end date. As for the calories, I'm choosing to believe they don't count during the holidays. #6549. Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and plan on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”

Whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

The first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have big ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

My favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

Marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that showed me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from New England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

There was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

While my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was big sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6546. Flambéed French Onion Crêpes

“As much as I appreciate a classic like crêpes Suzette, I also love a cheeky little twist!” says New York City pastry chef and cookbook author Caroline Schiff. Here, she takes the traditional dessert on a 180-degree ride to the savory side and nods to another classic along the way: French onion soup. She ditches the citrusy butter sauce in favor of golden caramelized onions and gloriously gooey gruyère, but keeps the drama by adding a splash of sherry and igniting it before serving.

#6545. Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too quickly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in our August 2023 issue and has been updated with additional guidance. Head this way for more of our favorite pecan recipes →

#6544. Ciara Has One Holiday Cooking Rule & You Really Don't Want To Break It

She's all for getting creative with Oreos, although she has much stronger feelings about the rest of the menu.

Ciara has one request for whoever’s in charge of Christmas dinner: Please, whatever you do, make sure you’re up for the assignment. She’s willing to embrace a little holiday mess, but apparently, there’s a limit to how far that generosity extends into the kitchen.

“All I know is you better not burn no turkey. That’s a culinary crime,” the Grammy-winning singer told Delish. And if you're cooking without a backup bird? You might want to pay especially close attention to that oven. “You better get it right on the first try.”

Ciara, a mom of four, certainly understands how quickly the festivities can get away from you. “Christmas in our house is full of love, excitement and a little chaos,” she said in a statement. But when it comes to the actual Christmas menu, she’s got some traditions she’s pretty attached to, many of which go all the way back to her childhood in Atlanta, Georgia.

"If you know one thing about us ATLians, you have Thanksgiving on Christmas. The same meal comes back around again," she told Delish.

And we’re talking a serious Southern spread: turkey legs, mac and cheese, candied yams, collard greens, chitlins, and pig feet. She's no longer making pig feet these days, but the other familiar favorites have stuck around. Ciara says those dishes still “make me very happy,” which is as good a reason as any to keep a family tradition going.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

#6543. Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, New York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.)

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she says. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, says that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6540. 7 Simple Steps for Winterizing Your Lawn Mower

You can’t just park it in the shed and forget it. Both gas-powered and cordless mowers need to be prepared for winter storage.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Somehow the end of the year is upon us and mowing season is winding down. And while you should still be mowing your lawn until the first hard frost hits, soon it’ll be time to retire it for the winter, and you get to give that chore a rest for a bit. But you can’t just store the mower in the shed and forget about it. To ensure your lawn mower is ready to go next season, you need to winterize it before sending it into hibernation.

Winterizing is especially important for gas-powered mowers, which have engines that need fuel, oil, and an air filter to run properly. You should do some light maintenance on them before the cold weather arrives. While cordless electric lawn mowers are easier to maintain, there are still a few steps you should take before storing them away.

Here are our tips for winterizing any lawn mower so it’s ready to go in the spring. Note that you don’t have to do them in this exact order; for example, you might want to leave fuel stabilization until later in the process, but we wanted to keep it at the top, since it’s one of the most important steps.

Prepping your gas-powered lawn mower for winter storage isn’t hard; there are just several things to consider, and if you cover them all, it should only take an hour or so. You will be dealing with engine fluids, however, so choose a work area and clothing that you don’t mind getting dirty.

When left for long periods, gasoline can become “stale,” meaning it evaporates and oxidizes, making it less combustible. It can also create residues that could damage the engine. Also, the ethanol found in most gasoline can break down if left to sit, causing performance issues and attracting water that can cause corrosion (one of the reasons ethanol-free gas is better for lawn mowers).

You can avoid the problems by adding a fuel stabilizer, but if there is any air in the tank, it’s not a perfect solution. Meanwhile, siphoning the gas from the tank is not truly going to remove all of it, so here’s our advice, in steps:

Not everyone will recommend this method, but we believe that, since a full tank has almost no air in it, there is little space for fuel to evaporate or for condensation to form due to temperature changes. Therefore, you are less likely to encounter problems than if you had drained the tank.

Large gas-powered mowers, such as lawn tractors and zero-turn mowers, typically have a battery to power the starter, lights, and other accessories. Gas walk-behind mowers with an electric start feature will also have a battery. It’s a good idea to remove it for the winter and clean it to remove corrosion on the terminals or battery posts. When performing this task, wear nitrile gloves and eye protection. If your battery has a lot of corrosion, you don't want to remove it in a way that it gets airborne. You can use a solution of water and baking soda to neutralize the corrosion and wipe it off with a rag or microfiber cloth.

Most experts recommend replacing your spark plug every year. Changing your spark plug can vary depending on the model of lawn mower you own, so always consult your manual. If you do not feel it’s necessary to replace it, at least remove it to check for any damage. If you see a lot of carbon buildup, rust, or cracks, it’s best to change it.

Drain the oil from the mower after letting it run for 5 minutes—warm oil flows more easily. For walk-behind mowers, this will require you to tip the mower over, so it’s probably better to remove the gas first or at least make sure the gas tank is securely sealed. When tipping the mower, the carburetor and air filter sections should be facing upward to avoid oil contamination—since the oil spout is usually on the opposite side of the carb and filter, you’ll naturally be following this rule anyway. But it’s good advice for when you tip the mower to clean the underside of the deck as well.

This is pretty easy to do, but it helps to know what the filter is made of. Paper and fiber filters should be replaced. If it’s a foam filter element, you can use water and Dawn dish soap, but make sure to rinse it well and let it air dry completely before reinstalling it.

You should be cleaning your mower deck throughout the summer, but if not, make a point to do it before storing it; otherwise, the caked-on grass may cause corrosion or attract bugs and vermin. As mentioned above, make sure to tip your mower so that the air box and carburetor are on the high side to avoid fuel contamination.

After you’ve completed the task of cleaning the deck, it’s a good idea to wipe down your engine with a damp cloth, removing any dirt or debris, and dry it with another towel.

The end of the season is a good time to sharpen your mower blade or replace it altogether. You can take it to a lawn mower repair shop to have it done, but if you have a few basic tools, it’s very simple to do it yourself.

The beauty of a cordless mower is that there’s less maintenance you need to perform. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t steps to take before storing it away for winter.

Batteries are the lifeblood of a cordless mower, so you need to take care of them. Don’t leave them in the mower over winter, especially if you’re keeping it in an uninsulated shed that sees cold temperatures. Remove your batteries and charge them to between 40 and 60 percent. Check the charge level every two months or so, as lithium-ion batteries lose power over time. Partially recharge the batteries if they dip close to 20 percent or lower.

Store your batteries in a cool, dark place such as a basement or insulated garage (but not near a furnace or heat source). For a riding mower that has a built-in battery you cannot remove, park it in a garage or at least a covered area. If stored in a place that gets below freezing, don’t leave it on a charger or try to recharge it, as some batteries (lithium-ion) should not be charged below 32 degrees Fahrenheit. Get it to a warmer place or wait until a warmer day.

This isn’t much different from how you do it for a gas mower; just be careful if using water to do any cleaning, as this can potentially damage electrical components. Also, be sure to remove the batteries before you do any kind of cleaning on a cordless mower.

Again, this isn’t a different process than a gas mower; just make sure the batteries are removed first to avoid the chance of the mower starting up accidentally.

#6538. Ina Garten’s Dancing With The Stars Confession Has Me Mourning What Could’ve Been

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

“Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”

With which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

#6537. The Maldon Salt Scandal, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.)

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a new study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its big flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

As a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) officially announced its decision to revoke the United States' measles elimination status on Nov. 17, 2026. The week prior, the Wall Street Journal reported that the PAHO had reached that decision.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6533. Grand Theft Auto Started as a Broken Racing Game No One Liked. Then the Code Malfunctioned—Brilliantly.

One programming error turned Pac-Man-style police into maniac cops, and the rest is gaming history.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s spanned the lifecycle of countless gaming consoles, survived multiple scandals, and even withstood a Congressional investigation. The Grand Theft Auto franchise is seemingly unkillable. Not even a more-than-a-decade wait for the latest installment, Grand Theft Auto VI, could dull the rabid hunger the global gaming community has for the series of open world crime games.

Yet, the massive franchise was almost over before it began. The original Grand Theft Auto, it turns out, was on the proverbial chopping block in the middle of its development. It was only through a few fateful glitches that developers saw what they really had on their hands.

“It was awful,” former creative director Gary Penn recalled in an interview quoted by Game Informer. “It never really felt like it was going anywhere.” At the time, in 1994, the game wasn’t even called Grand Theft Auto,—it went by the much tamer moniker Race’n’Chase. Its developers, now known as Rockstar North, were then a small Scottish studio called DMA Design Ltd. They were best known at the time for a cute, family-friendly (if mildly macabre) PC game called Lemmings.

“The aim of Race’n’Chase,” read a March 1995 design document, “...is to produce a fun, addictive and fast multi-player car racing and crashing game which uses a novel graphics method.” The problem was, the game they were working on was neither fun nor addictive. The car crashes, for one, were a nightmare. “They just didn’t work,” programmer Mike Dailly told The Guardian. “The code was like spaghetti junction.”

Then there was the matter of the game’s central premise. Originally, Race’n’Chase was meant to be a top-down game where you could play as either the criminals or the police in pursuit, but the developers found that the latter element needed to be excised “’cause nobody wanted to play the cops.”

Even worse, as the developers tried to deal these design challenges, they were missing key deadlines, and their counterparts in America were getting impatient. “Every week they wanted to kill this game,” recalled level designer Paul Farley in a video for The Guardian. “We’d have to kind of argue to keep it going.”

Then something broke. And it was the best thing that ever happened to them.

The game had refocused around the criminal element, with the police now pursuing the player in a manner inspired by, of all things, the ghosts in Pac-Man. “Then one day,” Penn recounted, “I think it was a bug, the police suddenly became mental and aggressive. Everybody suddenly went, ‘Hey this is actually pretty cool. There’s something in this, this is working.’”

That malfunction switched things from Pac-Man ghosts to maniac cops—and recontextualized the entire game in the developers’ minds. “It was less about the mission stuff, which we always thought was another mess, and more about just general play—just being able to p**s around.”

The developers leaned into the freedom of the game’s sprawling digital city, focusing less on what players could accomplish and more on what they could get away with. In that moment, Race’n’Chase became Grand Theft Auto in all but name. Team members went home at night to watch American action fare like Speed and The A-Team, then came back the next day to pitch scenes from them as missions players could pick up at Liberty City’s trademark phone booths. Most importantly, they started seeing bugs not as roadblocks, but as launching pads.

Later in development, another glitch caused groups of NPC pedestrians to “start following one person around,” Farley recalled, much like the marching creatures in DMA’s previous hit, Lemmings. “We thought: ‘Can we use this? What sort of people walk around in a long line like that?’ And we thought of Hare Krishnas.” Rather than do some drastic rewrite of the code, they just tweaked the look of the pedestrians’ sprites, and got the game out to the public.

The game was famously met with controversy after its release because of its violent content, but that uproar actually played into the game’s marketing, and it became a massive financial success for the small Scottish studio. Grand Theft Auto has gone on to become one of the best-selling video game franchises in history, a title sure to be cemented with the release of the notably “sick day inducing” Grand Theft Auto VI.

And none of it would have happened without a single, fateful glitch.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. #6532. The Best Recipes to Bring to a Potluck, According to Eater Editors

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a big party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

Dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with big flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter
