#6469. The 9 Best Dishwashers of 2026

Our top recommendations from Bosch, Whirlpool, Midea, and more can knock out dishes with minimal disruption.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re tired of scrubbing pots and pans by hand, a good dishwasher is one of the best investments you can make for your home. The latest dishwasher models are smarter, quieter, and more efficient than previous generations, with soil-sensing cycles that adapt to your load, adjustable racks to accommodate dishes of all sizes, and quiet motors that won’t disrupt movie night. It’s the same kind of quality-of-life upgrade you get from buying a washing machine. Once you have one, it’s hard to imagine life without it.

Whether you’re replacing an aging unit or adding one to your home, the best dishwashers can make your kitchen routine easier. They may even help you save money on your water bill, too. To help narrow down your options, we focused on aspects like reliability, cleaning performance, and drying power, so your dishes come out spotless and ready to put away.

Adding a dishwasher to your home is an important decision, especially since it’s something you’ll be using a few times per week. To find the best models, we researched the top-rated machines from trusted brands like Bosch, Whirlpool, and GE, analyzing customer feedback and consulting expert reviews. We also relied on previous Popular Mechanics testing and extensive research to weigh the features that matter most in daily use.

Specifically, we prioritized quiet operation (favoring models under 50 decibels that won’t interrupt a conversation), adjustable racks and foldable tines, and proven cleaning performance. We then cross-referenced these insights with long-term reliability reports to ensure every pick on this list is built to last.

For our most recent update, we revisited the current dishwasher landscape to ensure every recommendation still holds up. We added new picks that offer a strong value, smart features, and a great fit for specific needs, like compact kitchens and busy households. We also re-evaluated our existing selections to confirm they remain competitive on price, performance, and availability.

The Bosch 300 Series checks all the right boxes as a top dishwasher. This front-control model cleans thoroughly with seven cycles, and it uses sensors and targeted spray arms to track soil and adjust as it runs. It’s quiet at 46 decibels, so you can run a cycle anytime without it interrupting your dinner conversation.

Storage is flexible, too. You get a standard third rack for utensils and other small items, plus a middle rack that adjusts to nine positions to make room for pots below and stemware above. Fold-down tines on the upper and lower racks accommodate lids and other cookware, and all three racks move smoothly. It also uses a condensation system for drying and leak protection that can automatically stop water intake if it detects a possible leak.

Other features include the ability to control and monitor cycles from your phone and hands-free voice control when paired with Amazon Alexa or Google Home. We only wish it had an auto-open door drying feature to top it all off, but this isn’t a major con by any means.

For around $500, the Frigidaire top control dishwasher is a dependable, modern dishwasher that offers Energy Star efficiency, a quick wash cycle, and a DishSense feature that helps adjust the wash based on how dirty the dishes are.

Meanwhile, Frigidaire’s Maxdry feature cranks up the heat for noticeably better drying than most entry-level models, so you’re not hand-drying half the load afterward. The fingerprint-resistant stainless steel finish also does a nice job of hiding smudges, helping it look cleaner for longer. It has a child lock, delay start, and a removable silverware basket, rounding out a feature set that feels surprisingly robust for a budget pick.

At 52 decibels, it won’t compete with high-end models that offer quieter performance, but it’s perfectly acceptable at this price point.

This dishwasher has nearly everything you want: a third rack, an adjustable second rack, and a handful of cycle options to thoroughly clean your dishes, including a quick wash and a high-temperature wash that helps remove grease. It also offers enhanced, fan-powered drying technology that ensures your cookware doesn’t come out damp. At 51 decibels, it’s not the loudest, but not the quietest either.

Other notable features include a presoak cycle to clean off stubborn food and folding tines to fit larger items like mixing bowls and large pots. Unfortunately, there is no WiFi support or app compatibility, limiting the dishwasher’s convenience compared to other models.

Dishwashers are more flexible than ever with multiple racks and ample space for efficient organization. This Midea top-control model stands out with a third rack and spray arms for each level, making it easy to customize the interior to get thorough cleaning.

You can raise or lower the middle rack by up to 2 inches to make room for big pots, baking sheets, or tall plates below, so you don’t have to go through the effort of hand-washing cumbersome dishes. The Midea also features a dedicated third rack for utensils and flat cooking tools, along with jets that spray directly into reusable water bottles.

Beyond organization, a three-stage drying system combines heated dry, auto-open door, and air circulation, so you’re not toweling dishes off after the cycle finishes. And with a 47 decibel sound rating, it runs quietly enough that it won’t disrupt conversations. The only thing we noticed was that some reviewers had complaints about the latch on the door rusting, and the racks breaking. That said, it may be less reliable in the long-term compared to higher-end models.

If you actually want the “smart” part of a smart dishwasher to pull its weight, this LG model is an easy standout. We like that WiFi and LG’s ThinQ app let you fire up or pause a cycle from the couch, check how much time is left, and get pinged when it’s done, while Alexa and Google Assistant support hands-free control. The app keeps an eye on water supply, drainage, and leaks, and sends alerts if something looks off. It also nudges you when it’s time for routine maintenance.

The smart features extend to how it runs, too. A sensor wash cycle automatically adjusts time and water based on how dirty your dishes actually are. LG’s one-hour wash and dry program also uses four multi-directional spray arms for deeper cleaning and then circulates heated air throughout the tub for faster drying.

An auto-vent feature pops the door open slightly at the end of a cycle to vent steam, and a status light projects onto the floor so you’re able to see when it’s done at a glance. These features combine to make cleaning your dishes a little smarter and less painful.

While the upper rack gets fold-down tines for odd-shaped glassware and bowls, the lower rack doesn’t, so it’s a bit trickier to load large pans and bakeware than on models with fully flexible lower racks. However, if you normally hand wash large pots and pans, this may not be an issue.

The Whirlpool Eco Series 24-Inch Top Control Dishwasher is a great pick for families that go through dishes like a small restaurant. It’s built to keep up with real-life cleanup, using a three-rack layout so you can load more dishes in one go. Below, the lower rack has fold-down tines for bulky cookware, making it easier to run a full day’s worth of dishes.

The Sensor cycle uses AI technology to monitor soil level, load size, and water temperature, then adjusts as it goes. There are also cycles that add soak time and longer wash phases to help reduce the need for pre-scrubbing. A sanitizer rinse option targets food-borne bacteria, while a high temperature wash helps cut through grease. Meanwhile, the combination of heated and condensation drying features mean you’ll have dishes that are ready to put away when the cycle finishes.

There is no app control or remote monitoring features, but this dishwasher does offer a fingerprint-resistant stainless exterior and a relatively quiet sound rating of 47 decibels. That means you’ll be able to throw it on without ruining family movie night.

The GE Profile 18-Inch Top Control Built-in Dishwasher is great for smaller apartments where cabinet space is tight. It offers full-height racks, an adjustable upper rack, and room for everyday dishes, glasses, and cookware. With a three-level wash system, you don’t have to pre-wash anything in the sink. It even features a cycle that automatically adjusts time and water based on how much dirt it detects on your dishes.

The GE also features a stainless steel tub, an ADA-compliant low-profile design, and a sound rating of 47 decibels, so you can run it while you’re watching TV without having to raise the volume. There is no third rack, but it does have fold-down tines and a removable silverware basket, providing you with more flexibility when loading dishes. As someone who dealt with a basic 18-inch dishwasher at a previous apartment, the GE is a big upgrade.

The Midea 18-Inch Built-in Dishwasher is a great budget pick if you want a true built-in dishwasher in a small space without spending a premium price. At 18 inches wide with room for 8 place settings, it tucks into narrow apartment kitchens, bar nooks, or RV islands while still handling daily dishes for a small household.

You get six wash settings, including Heavy, ECO, and Quick, plus heated dry and a sanitize option. The stainless-steel tub feels more durable and premium than its price suggests, and users call out how quiet it is while running. The main trade-offs are a somewhat fussy lower rack for full-size plates and long normal-cycle times; however, if you’re prioritizing price, small-footprint installation, and solid cleaning over bells and whistles, this Midea is an excellent and affordable option.

Sometimes you don’t feel like washing a small amount of dishes by hand, but running a full cycle on a dishwasher feels like a waste of energy and water. This double-drawer model from GE is here to try to solve that problem.

You can run the two drawers separately or together, whether you need a quick rinse for a few plates and glasses, or a deeper clean for multiple place settings. This is especially convenient because you can continue loading dirty dishes while the other drawer runs through a cycle.

The dishwasher has six wash cycles, plus sanitizing and extra dry options. There are four adjustable shelves per drawer to accommodate plenty of dish and glass sizes. The detergent compartment is a little harder to fit pods, so you may be better off with a liquid or powder cleaner.

Some dishwashers might have to be hardwired to a dedicated circuit rather than using a plug-and-play connection. Hardwired dishwashers are more secure and permanent, while units with power cords are easier to install and offer more convenient disconnection in case of repairs. Both styles require access to a 120-volt, grounded outlet. Check the specs of the dishwasher you’re considering to ensure it aligns with your desired connection type.

Most households will be fine with a standard built-in dishwasher that slides under the counter and hooks into existing plumbing. However, portable and countertop models have come a long way and are now legitimate options for renters and small kitchens. Options like the GE Portable Freestanding Dishwasher, roll to the sink when needed and store away when you’re done.

Meanwhile, countertop dishwashers live on a counter or sturdy cart, and are ideal for smaller spaces like studios, where a full-size unit may not fit. Just know that compact models often compromise on features like noise reduction and capacity due to their smaller size.

For most households, dishwashers generally come in two widths: the standard 24-inch and the compact 18-inch. A 24-inch model is usually the best choice for families, having enough room for bulky cookware and larger loads. In contrast, an 18-inch model is a space-saving solution for small kitchens or narrow cabinet cutouts. I used an 18-inch machine in a previous apartment and found it filled up fast, forcing us to run cycles more frequently.

Manufacturers like to quote capacity in “place settings,” but what really matters day to day is interior flexibility and vertical space. Look for a tall tub design, which maximizes interior height so you can fit oversized items like baking sheets and pots on the bottom rack. A model with a third rack and an adjustable second rack, like the Whirlpool Eco Series Top Control Dishwasher, will give you enough flexibility to wash an entire day’s worth of cookware in a single load.

One of the biggest differentiators between modern dishwashers and older models is noise, which is measured in decibels (dB). Anything around 50 decibels or below is generally considered very quiet and shouldn’t overpower a normal conversation. Standard units that produce sound at around 51 decibels are more noticeable, especially during spray and drain cycles.

If you’re particularly sensitive to noise or often run the dishwasher at night outside of your energy company’s peak hours, look for models that promise quieter performance. Many of the newest dishwashers run quietly enough that you’ll barely notice them in the background. There have been multiple times when I’ve opened my Samsung dishwasher at home mid-cycle because I didn’t hear it running.

One of the most frustrating parts of using a dishwasher is opening the door to find wet dishes. Fortunately, modern dishwashers utilize several methods to ensure they come out bone-dry.

Some rely on traditional heated dry cycles, which raise interior temperature to evaporate moisture. Others take a more energy-efficient approach called condensation drying, where residual heat from the hot rinse water evaporates moisture against the cooler stainless steel walls. Newer models, like the Midea 24-Inch Top Control Built-in Dishwasher, have an auto-open feature, which automatically pops open the door at the end of the cycle to vent steam and ensure that even plastic containers dry completely.

Modern dishwashers pack more features than ever. When shopping around, you’ll see things like third racks for utensils, height-adjustable upper racks, soil sensors, foldable tines, and WiFi and app control. Many of these features give you the flexibility to load your dishes more efficiently, which means you can wash more items in a single load and are less likely to need to rewash plates or glasses.

Also consider where a dishwasher’s controls are (hidden on top versus front-facing), whether the tub is stainless steel, and other things that could potentially enhance your experience. Just remember that every added feature usually nudges the price up. Whatever you buy, make a habit of cleaning your dishwasher a couple times per year to keep it running like new.

Most households will be fine with a standard 24-inch dishwasher, which offers enough room for everyday dishes and larger cookware. But if you’re working with a smaller kitchen or apartment, an 18-inch model saves valuable real estate. “Your choice depends on available space, how many dishes you typically wash, and the size of the pans you cook with,” says Glenn Lewis, president of Mr. Appliance, a Neighborly company.

Yes, and it’s worth checking before you buy. “They need a dedicated 120-volt electrical connection, a water supply line, and a drain connection, all of which must meet local building codes for safe operation,” Lewis says. If you’re replacing an existing unit, the connections are likely already in place, but if you’re adding a dishwasher for the first time, you may need to hire a professional to set up the plumbing and electrical.

It’s possible, but proceed with caution. “You can if you have basic plumbing and electrical knowledge, but improper installation can lead to leaks or electrical issues, so many homeowners opt for professional installation,” Lewis says. If you’re swapping out an old unit and the connections are already there, a DIY install is more manageable. But for a first-time installation, professional help is usually the safer bet.

An Energy Star certification means the dishwasher meets strict efficiency standards that might save you money over time. “Energy Star-certified models use less water and electricity, not only to run the dishwasher but to heat the water used by the dishwasher,” Lewis says. “Lower energy means lower utility bills and reduced environmental impact over time.” If you’re choosing between two similar models, going with the Energy Star-certified option is usually the smarter long-term investment.

#6468. Why Did Early Humans Collect Strange Stones 500,000 Years Ago? Scientists Have a New Theory

Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.

A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else. Yet years later, that small object can bring back memories of where you were, who you were with, and what made the experience special. It’s a familiar human habit, and researchers now believe its origins may reach back nearly half a million years.

A new study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today. The researchers propose that these prehistoric keepsakes could have helped shape our ability to remember personal experiences and develop a sense of who we are.

The idea emerged from archaeological discoveries at several prehistoric sites in Israel, where researchers found colorful stones, unusual handaxes, and much older tools that appeared to have been collected despite offering no obvious practical benefit.

At Qesem Cave, for example, small, colorful pebbles had been brought in from different locations. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological patterns. Some were carefully shaped so that these distinctive features remained at the center, where they could be seen and touched.

Other discoveries offer an intriguing connection to the past. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, researchers identified older flint tools that had apparently been collected after their surfaces had changed with age. Although some were resharpened, much of their original surfaces and evidence of earlier workmanship remained intact.

Why would someone keep an old tool when they could make a new one? The researchers suggest that its age and appearance may have been part of its appeal. Just as an old family heirloom can carry meaning beyond its usefulness, these objects might have been valued for the experiences or histories associated with them.

Dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology explains the possibility:

“When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives. In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so important in shaping our identity.”

There may be a deeper psychological reason why such objects mattered. Our minds do not simply store experiences. They must also distinguish between things we personally experienced, stories we heard from others, and events we imagined.

The researchers propose that seeing or touching a familiar object could have helped early humans make those distinctions. A stone collected from a particular location, for instance, might have brought back a personal memory of being there.

That ability could have mattered well beyond individual recollection. Remembering encounters, alliances, gifts, mutual obligations, and rights connected to particular places helps people maintain relationships and cooperate. A keepsake could also be carried elsewhere and shown to others, potentially making a personal account more convincing and helping establish trust.

The researchers believe this behavior may have become especially useful as early humans faced changes in their environment.

Prof. Ran Barkai offers one possible explanation:

“The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop new hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle. Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”

Over many generations, the researchers suggest, keeping meaningful objects may have placed evolutionary pressure on the brain systems involved in identifying where memories come from and how reliable they are.

In this proposed scenario, objects and memory evolved together. As people increasingly used physical reminders of their experiences, the brain mechanisms supporting personal memory may have become more sophisticated.

That process could have contributed to the development of autobiographical memory, our ability to connect individual experiences into a continuing story of our lives. It is an important part of how we understand our identities and our relationships with others.

The researchers emphasize that their interpretation remains a hypothesis. An unusual stone or carefully preserved tool does not necessarily prove that its owner associated it with a personal memory. The archaeological evidence cannot reveal exactly what someone was thinking hundreds of thousands of years ago.

However, the findings suggest that the habit of keeping meaningful objects may date back roughly 500,000 years, long before written records or photographs.

And if the researchers’ interpretation is correct, the simple act of keeping a stone from a memorable place may once have played a role in the evolution of how humans remember their lives.

Reference: “Homo Memorabiliaxis: Souvenirs and the Evolution of Autobiographical Memory and Self” by Ran Barkai, Ella Assaf, Bar Efrati, Tal Simon, Liad Mudrik and Yoav Ram, 19 October 2026, Evolutionary Anthropology: Issues, News, and Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/evan.70051

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."

#6466. The Origins of Wealth Inequality May Go Back 5,000 Years, Ancient Graves Reveal

The roots of inherited privilege may reach back thousands of years, with ancient graves revealing how one European community gradually became more divided by wealth and status.

Among nearly 300 prehistoric graves examined in Bohemia, the richest belonged to a young girl. Buried alongside her was an exceptionally rare copper neck ring, an object that raises an intriguing question about life thousands of years ago. Was she born into a wealthy family, or did her elaborate burial reflect something else about how her community valued status?

For archaeologists, questions like these are difficult to answer because prehistoric societies left behind no census records, tax registers, or written accounts of who held wealth and power.

A new archaeological method is helping researchers piece together that missing history by examining how people buried their dead. Developed by University of Copenhagen archaeologist Mikkel Nørtoft during his PhD research, QuantWealth combines multiple forms of archaeological evidence to reconstruct social status, displays of wealth, and inequality. In a study published in the Journal of Neolithic Archaeology, Nørtoft and his colleague Adam B. Rohrlach applied the method to 296 graves belonging to the Corded Ware culture in present-day Bohemia, dating from approximately 2900 to 2300 BCE.

The researchers examined burial practices and grave goods alongside genetic ancestry, Y-chromosome patterns that trace paternal lineages, and skeletal evidence of age, sex, and pathological conditions. By comparing these different clues, they could investigate how social differences changed across several centuries. The findings suggest that inequality developed gradually rather than emerging as a firmly established social hierarchy when migrants from the eastern European steppe settled in the region.

The Corded Ware culture formed part of a much larger transformation in prehistoric Europe, when populations migrating from the steppe helped spread early Indo-European dialects across the continent. Archaeologists have debated whether these newcomers also introduced strongly patriarchal societies in which wealth and power passed primarily through family lines. The evidence from Bohemia points toward a more complicated history.

“Archaeologists have long debated whether steppe populations migrating across Europe from Ukraine brought with them a highly unequal social system and patriarchy. Our results suggest a much more dynamic picture, where social differences developed gradually. Achieving status through life-actions appears to have been more important than through inheritance, at least during the first 400 years”, says Nørtoft, the study’s lead author.

During the earliest period, approximately 2900 to 2700 BCE, burial practices suggest that the newly established communities placed considerable emphasis on shared traditions. Differences in grave wealth were relatively small and largely associated with age. There was little evidence of pronounced gender inequality, and power appeared to be distributed among several paternal lineages with steppe ancestry.

Nørtoft connects this early pattern to the circumstances surrounding the migrants’ arrival in Central Europe.

“Following a few harsh years of ‘dark sun’ clouded by a devastating volcanic eruption 2,900 BCE, the earliest herder communities, settling in Bohemia around 2,900-2,700 BCE, seem to have focused mostly on building social cohesion across this new network of migrants in Central Europe. In Bohemia, they did this through shared burial rituals, and building earthen mounds, but with few grave goods,” Mikkel Nørtoft explains.

Between approximately 2700 and 2500 BCE, however, burial customs began to change. The appearance of a new paternal lineage coincided with increasingly elaborate funerals, including greater concentrations of prestigious objects and meat offerings. Exchange networks expanded, and differences between male and female burials became more pronounced.

Adult men were particularly likely to receive richly furnished graves, while younger adults became increasingly common among those buried. Despite this growing competition for status, the skeletal evidence did not show a clear corresponding increase in injuries associated with violence.

The final phase, spanning roughly 2500 to 2300 BCE, brought further changes. One paternal lineage had become dominant in the burial record, and a small number of children received unusually wealthy burials. Because children had less opportunity to accumulate status through their own accomplishments, these graves raise the possibility that some families had begun passing social advantages between generations.

“In the final phase, roughly 2,500-2,300 BCE, we see a few rich displays of family wealth through children, and the previously new lineage now dominated the burial record. So maybe the new lineage had gained the most followers and power through the competitive burial parties, and their descendants were now competing among themselves,” Mikkel Nørtoft points out and adds:

“The few rich child graves and this prevailing lineage could indicate more inherited wealth and emerging traits of persistent inequality. Ethnographic parallels could also support the idea that parents adorned their children with ornaments to increase their social value in future marriage exchange. Brides often moved into the husband’s household in Corded Ware societies, and bridewealth or dowry is preserved in early Indo-European vocabulary, and historically common in Indo-European societies.”

The extraordinarily rich grave of a young girl at Čachovice offers a particularly striking example of this possible shift. It was the wealthiest burial among all 296 graves examined and contained an extremely rare copper neck ring. Similar neck ornaments, known as torcs, became widespread symbols of upper-class status during the later European Bronze and Iron Ages. The researchers suggest that objects placed in children’s graves may sometimes have reflected family standing or efforts to enhance their social value in future marriage arrangements, although these interpretations remain uncertain.

Taken together, the changing burial patterns suggest that competition for prestige may have gradually created more lasting social divisions within Corded Ware communities. The possibility that wealth and status were becoming hereditary is especially significant because later Bronze Age societies provide evidence of enduring family dynasties. Whether the developments in Bohemia represented early steps toward those systems remains an open question.

Researchers will need additional archaeological and genetic evidence from both the Corded Ware culture and the related Bell Beaker culture, which subsequently replaced it in Central Europe, to determine how closely burial wealth corresponded to inherited family status. The study demonstrates how archaeological evidence, ancient DNA, and linguistic history can be combined to investigate social changes that written records cannot document.

“We now have a correlation between changing Y-haplogroup lineages and unequal burial wealth display in one region, but we need more DNA data to confirm this at the family level, and elsewhere,” explains Nørtoft.

Reference: “Cooperation and Competition: Changes in Wealth, Power, and Patrilines in the Czech Corded Ware Culture” by Mikkel Nørtoft and Adam B. Rohrlach, November 2026, Journal of Neolithic Archaeology. DOI: 10.12766/jna.2026.7

#6465. Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

"We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," said Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

“With advances in AI creating new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster said in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking said.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a company that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

He's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

“He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary says.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

#6464. The 8 Best Cordless Stick Vacuums Are Convenient, Versatile, and Work Well on Carpets Too

These lightweight, easy-to-store models get the job done with multiple attachments and powerful motors.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A cordless stick vacuum has the potential to be one of the most convenient cleaning tools in your home. These lightweight machines make it easy to clean up pet hair from area rugs and hidden dust along baseboards, without having to haul out an upright vacuum or wrestling with a power cord. Most models also convert into handheld vacuums, giving you more flexibility to clean furniture, stairs, and other hard-to-reach spots.

Suction power, battery life, maneuverability, and dustbin capacities vary between models, so the right cordless stick vacuum ultimately depends on your home’s flooring, how much debris you’re dealing with, and the features that will actually make your cleaning routine easier.

We’ve rounded up the best cordless stick vacuums worth considering based on our hands-on experience, with options for everything from everyday maintenance to deeper carpet cleaning.

🔎 Looking for more ways to keep your floors and furniture clean? Check out our stories on the best robot vacuums, the best vacuums for pet hair, the best vacuums for hardwood floors, and the best handheld vacuums.

I’ve spent considerable time researching, testing, and vetting all types of vacuums, so I’ve developed a pretty good understanding of what separates a genuinely useful appliance from one that is just going to take up space in your storage closet. I’ve evaluated a wide range of models, including full-size uprights, canister vacuums, robot, and handheld models vacuums, paying close attention to performance, ease of use, and features that can really make a difference in a your regular cleaning routine.

When testing cordless stick vacuums, we assessed how well each model could handle common household debris, its ability to transition between carpet and hardwood floors, and how easy it was to move around furniture and into tighter spaces. We also looked at the practical considerations like battery life, suction power, dustbin capacity, weight, filtration, and included attachments.

Beyond just how the vacuum cleans, we also considered the overall experience for an owner. Removable batteries, self-cleaning docking stations, washable filters, and easy-to-empty dustbins can also make daily vacuuming less of a drag. The below recommendations are both powerful and dependable for a wide range of cleaning needs and surface types.

The Dyson V15 Detect is the most expensive stick vacuum in our lineup, but if you can stomach the price tag, you’ll get a cordless stick vacuum that (quite literally) leaves the competition in the dust across the board. It delivers top-notch performance on floors and carpets to tackle everything from fine dust and pet dander to larger debris.

Its motor spins up to 125,000 rpm and it comes with two cleaning heads, including an upgraded version of the brand’s “fluffy” head that features a green laser headlight to detect fine dust. During testing, we found that being able to switch from cordless to handheld made it easier to transition from tackling small messes to deeper cleaning sessions.

The auto mode is a nice feature for conserving battery life, as this model only runs for about an hour off one charge. Another highlight is the motorized pet tool.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

The PowerClean FurFinder is a more affordable alternative to the PowerClean FurGuard we recommend, but that doesn’t mean you have to give up useful features.

This cordless stick vacuum is intended for use on a variety of floor types, and the flat-lay construction makes cleaning under furniture much more accessible. The vacuum also stands up on its own which leads to fewer interruptions during a cleaning session.

We love that both the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment come with headlights because it makes it a lot easier to see hidden dirt and debris. The brush roll is a tangle-free design, and the FurFinder is equipped with a HEPA filter for trapping small particles and allergens.

The motor on this vacuum is less powerful than the PowerClean, but it still provides plenty of suction for daily household cleaning.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurFinder Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Since we’re big fans of the Shark AZ2002 Vertex upright vacuum for deep and thorough cleans, it’s no surprise that we like the cordless model in this lineup, too. The brush roll is excellent at pulling hair and large debris from carpets, as well as polishing up your hardwood floors. The cordless stick vacuum features an advertised runtime of 60 minutes.

It also offers a HEPA filtration system and converts to a hand vac, and it also bends at the center of the wand to get around and under furniture. The Vertex comes with plenty of accessories for cleaning a variety of spaces. However, this may not be the best choice if you regularly clean stairs, as the cordless vacuum weighs roughly nine pounds—significantly more than other vacuums we cover.

I have two cats and live with my partner, which means there is plenty of mess to go around, from pet hair and dust to tracked-in dirt. I appreciate all the thoughtful features of the Tineco Station 5 because they make daily maintenance much easier.

Automatic suction adjustment has proved useful on my laminate and tile floors. I can hear when the motor gets a boost of power in a particularly dirty area, and it helps on carpets and area rugs where crumbs and debris tends to get trapped between the fibers. Add to that a green laser light for dust detection and you’ll hardly ever miss a spot.

I particularly like the base station. It has a 2.5-liter capacity, and after two months of using the Station 5, I still haven’t had to empty it. When I dock the vacuum onto the base, it automatically empties the onboard dustbin, cleans the floorhead brush roll, and charges the vacuum. Combined, these intuitive features make for a cleaning routine that is virtually hands-free.

Full Tineco Pure ONE Station 5 Pro Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Even though the Dyson V11 Origin came out several years ago, that doesn’t mean this model has stopped being useful.

The motorbar cleaner head works exceptionally well on carpet, successfully agitating fibers to pull up embedded dirt, dander, and hair. Suction is equally impressive, and there are three power modes depending on the level of cleaning you need. I ran the vacuum on medium most of the time, but I used boost occasionally whenever an area needed the extra attention.

This model doesn’t come with a soft roller brush vacuum head, and while it does work on all floor types, it can be loud on hardwood and laminate. But if your home is mostly carpet, this is a cordless stick vacuum I would reach for.

Full Dyson V11 Origin Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Our tester has a busy household six pets, so there’s no question that she’s regularly cleaning up after her animals. Pulling out the upright vacuum daily isn’t convenient, so she turned to the Levoit LVAC-300 to fill the gap.

This cordless stick vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—and she was able to cycle through each right from the handle depending on how much suction power she needed. She found that the vacuum was able to pick up litter and sand on different surfaces and between thresholds with ease.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but she was disappointed that there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself. The LVAC-300 runs for up to 60 minutes depending on what mode you’re using, and the HEPA filter is a great feature if you have animals.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

I used the Bissell PowerClean FurGuard across my apartment to clean laminate floors, area rugs, carpeting, and upholstery, and I fell in love with several features.

The vacuum lays completely flat, making it really easy to get underneath furniture, and the swivel steering helps guide the FurGuard around tight spaces. Being a pet owner, I appreciate that the brush roll is tangle-free, so I don’t have to cut hair loose as often as I would with a standard, bristled brush roll.

Other highlights were lights on the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment. I was able to see collected dirt and debris that I would normally miss on hardwood flooring, carpet, and furniture. I also like that this model is designed to be self-standing.

It’s hard to come by a cordless stick vacuum that you don’t have to re-mount or set on the ground during your cleaning session. With this model, I was able to stop and start with ease.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurGuard Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We recently got our hands on one of the latest cordless stick vacuums from Shark, and we were impressed by the PowerDetect’s construction. The pole has a hinge in the center and when you release it, the vacuum bends to extend under furniture and hard-to-reach places. Our tester didn’t have to kneel down or adjust angles while he was cleaning thanks to the intuitive design.

Beyond that, the PowerDetect vacuum uses sensors on the bottom of the floor head to discern between surface types, and adjusts suction power when needed. During testing, the motor could be heard transitioning speeds when used on hardwood and shag carpet.

This vacuum also comes with a docking station, which automates the process of emptying out the dustbin. The vacuum itself can’t hold that much debris onboard, so it’s nice having a one-stop-shop for clearing out the bagless canister during a cleaning session. It’s a little heavy for a cordless stick vacuum, but it still gets the job done.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Not every cordless stick vacuum we test ends up in this roundup. However, these other models still perform well and are reliable recommendations:

Levoit Aero Cordless Vacuum Cleaner: The Tineco we’ve included above has more raw suction power, reaching up to 27,000Pa versus the 14,000Pa of the Levoit. However, one of the highlights of the Aero is the 3.5-liter-capacity dust bag in the docking station. Depending on your cleaning frequency, you could potentially go months without having to empty and replace it, and this design is better for keeping dust and dander from being expelled back into the air.

Dyson Gen5Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum: This cordless stick vacuum certainly commands a premium price, and you get a lot of the same features as the Dyson V15 Detect we recommend above, such as an LCD display screen, the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, and pet hair attachments. If you’re an allergy sufferer, you may prefer the Gen5Detect because its filtration system captures particles down to 0.1 microns, while the V15 filters down to just 0.3 microns. Plus, runtime is slightly longer on the Gen5Detect.

The main advantages of owning a cordless stick vacuum are easy portability and storage. But what you trade for the convenience is battery life and runtime. Most models clean from 30 to 60 minutes, but that’s also dependent on what setting you’re using. If you’re running the vacuum on its highest speed the entire time, it might die faster. Be wary of manufacturers’ advertised total runtime because it may represent performance on the lowest setting or using two fully charged batteries, for instance. Battery charging should also be factored in, so plan your cleaning session accordingly so you don’t lose power in the middle of a floor swipe.

Like we mentioned earlier, the dustbins on cordless stick vacuums are significantly smaller than those of an upright or canister unit. You should consider your cleaning habits and the spaces you usually vacuum to find a model that aligns with your needs. If you live in an apartment or are using the cordless vac to supplement your other cleaning supplies, then a dustbin with at least half a liter capacity should do. Some of the models we recommend hold up to one liter of debris, which helps limit the number of trips to the trash can.

Although not a necessity, having a good amount of attachments with your vacuum is especially helpful for cleaning hard-to-reach places or targeting specific issues. Crevice tools pick up dirt and dander from corners and couch cushions, while bristled brushes and motorized pet tools agitate and lift hair and fur that’s been embedded into upholstery.

A good filtration system helps combat allergens such as dust and pet dander that are being kicked up by a vacuum. The best option is a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. A fully sealed or multi-step filtration system also has the potential to trap a wide variety of airborne allergens without releasing them back into your home.

Cordless vacuums are very effective at picking up pet hair, especially models designed with high suction power and specialized brush rolls. Some of the models we recommend include motorized attachments that lift embedded hair from upholstery and carpets. Anti-tangle vacuum heads are also a key feature that helps prevent hair from wrapping around the brush roll. While not all models perform equally, a high-quality cordless stick vacuum is able to handle pet hair just as well as traditional versions.

The lifespan of these vacuums typically lasts from three to five years, depending on usage, build quality, and maintenance. Battery performance plays a major role, since lithium-ion batteries start to lose capacity over time.

Avoiding overcharging and storing the vacuum properly could help extend the battery life significantly. Running regular maintenance like cleaning the vacuum filters and emptying the dustbin completely preserves suction and functionality. Higher-end models often last longer due to better materials and replaceable parts, but either price point has potential to last for years with proper care.

Modern designs are increasingly more effective at cleaning many surface types, including rugs and carpets. Advances in battery tech and general efficiency have allowed for strong suction performance that is comparable to corded models. Adjustable power modes allow for deeper cleaning on thicker carpets, and multi-roller and motorized brush heads agitate fibers to loosen dirt and debris.

Performance may vary depending on the type of flooring. Some vacuums are designed to work on low-to-medium pile carpets, while others are able to handle high-pile. It’s best to consult the listed features and specs of the model you’re considering to ensure it aligns with the flooring types in your home.

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

#6463. Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

During angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the new analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

Earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

The central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

“When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” said Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

“We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”

These results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a new randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

The researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

The research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala said considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

Reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488

Up to 15 shooting stars per hour may be visible as the Leonids peak under dark skies tonight (Nov. 16 - 17), with the moon setting before the best viewing hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky.

Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society.

Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails.

The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky.

A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. Don't use binoculars or a telescope during a meteor shower; they will only restrict your view. However, you can try your hand at photographing the shower with your smartphone or a good astrophotography camera.

The Leonids are produced by tiny particles of dust and debris left behind in the inner solar system by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which takes about 33 years to orbit the sun and is about 2.2 miles (3.6 km) in diameter. Tempel-Tuttle last visited the inner solar system in 1998 and is due to return again in 2031.

Although no rapid-fire "meteor storms" are expected this year, the Leonids are famous for occasionally producing outbursts of 1,000 shooting stars per hour. Such storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002, according to the American Meteor Society. The next storm is expected to hit in 2099.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

After the Leonids, the next major meteor shower will be the Geminids, which peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. The Geminid meteor shower, which is caused by an asteroid rather than a comet, can produce up to 120 meteors per hour. This year, the Geminids will peak in dark skies, thanks to a slim crescent moon setting shortly after dark on Dec. 13.

#6461. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call)

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness."

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

He had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

"These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice."

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

#6460. Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find New Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a new Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

For example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

The method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” says Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

The approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” says Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very important in treatment decisions.”

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” says Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”

The risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

Reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292
